title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Malaysia: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Malaysia: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Malaysia: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: When a Malaysian citizen dies in Malaysia, administrative procedures depend on both statutory civil registration and Malaysia's dual-system inheritance framework distinguishing Muslims and non-Muslims, as well as regional civil-registration rules between Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah, and Sarawak. Promptly securing medical clearance, registering the death, and identifying which estate forum applies prevents frozen accounts and delayed property transfers. This checklist summarizes the core official procedures based on Malaysian statutes and public agencies [1][2][4].

steps.title: Immediate medical certification and police reporting
steps.html:
• Death in a hospital: The attending medical officer issues the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (MCCD) or burial/cremation permit document required to begin civil registration and body release [1][2].
  • Death at home or sudden/unexpected death: Under Malaysian procedure, report the death immediately to the nearest police station so a police officer can inspect the scene, arrange hospital post-mortem or forensic assessment if the cause is unclear, and issue the official police death report needed for civil registration [1][11].
  • Verify accuracy before leaving the clinic or police station: Check that the deceased's full name, MyKad number, date, time, and cause of death match identity records before filing with the civil registrar [1].

steps.title: Civil death registration and death certificates
steps.html:
• Seven-day ordinary registration rule in Peninsular Malaysia: Under the Births and Deaths Registration Act 1957 (Act 299), ordinary registration of a death in Peninsular Malaysia must be submitted within 7 days of death using Form JPN.LM02, after which Section 21 late-registration approval and fees apply (note that Sabah and Sarawak administer separate regional ordinances under the same national agency) [1][2].
  • Registration authority and documents: File at any National Registration Department (JPN) office with Form JPN.LM02, the medical certificate or police report, the deceased's original MyKad (which must be surrendered), and the informant's identity card; ordinary death certificates (Sijil Kematian) are issued without fee [1].
  • Foreign-language use and certified extracts: Request extra certified extracts at registration or later through National Registration Department (JPN) if multiple banks, insurers, and overseas authorities require originals [1][11].

steps.title: Burial, cremation, repatriation, and consular legalization
steps.html:
• Burial and cremation clearances: Cemeteries and crematoria require the municipal or police burial permit and certified death notification or death certificate before interment or cremation [1][11].
  • Malaysia is not an Apostille Convention party: According to the Hague Conference on Private International Law status table, Malaysia is not a Contracting Party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention, so Malaysian death certificates and court grants cannot receive an Apostille [9].
  • Consular legalization chain via Wisma Putra: Documents intended for use abroad must first be authenticated by the Consular Division of Ministry of Foreign Affairs Malaysia (Wisma Putra) in Putrajaya (with prior JPN verification/translation where required) and then legalized by the destination country's embassy or high commission in Malaysia [8][11].

steps.title: Provident fund, social security, tax, and ID closures
steps.html:
• Employees Provident Fund (KWSP / EPF) Death Withdrawal: Registered nominees (or estate administrators where no nomination exists, with simplified processing typically available up to RM25,000 before formal legal letters are required above that threshold) may apply in person at Employees Provident Fund (KWSP / EPF) using Form KWSP 9KM, the death certificate, and identity/relationship proof; eligible next-of-kin may also qualify for the one-off RM2,500 Death Assistance within 6 months of death [6].
  • Note on KWSP nominations by religion: For non-Muslim members, an EPF nominee takes beneficially even over a will; for Muslim members, a nominee acts solely as wasi (administrator) legally obliged to distribute funds to rightful Faraid heirs [6].
  • PERKESO / SOCSO survivor and funeral benefits: If the deceased was insured under Social Security Organisation (PERKESO / SOCSO), eligible dependents may claim the Survivors' Pension (Pencen Penakat) under the Invalidity Scheme alongside the Funeral Benefit (Faedah Pengurusan Mayat) of up to RM3,000 [7].

steps.title: Dual-system estate administration, probate, and property
steps.html:
• Muslims vs. non-Muslims jurisdiction: For Muslim decedents, inheritance follows Islamic Faraid law and heirs must obtain a Faraid Certificate from the Syariah Court before estate distribution orders can proceed, whereas non-Muslim estates are governed by the Wills Act 1959 (Act 346) if a valid will exists or the Distribution Act 1958 (Act 300) on intestacy (with an official distribution calculator hosted by MyGovernment) [3][10].
  • High Court, Small Estates (JKPTG), and AmanahRaya: Formal estates with a will require a High Court Grant of Probate; intestate estates involving immovable property up to RM5 million (under the amended Small Estates (Distribution) Act 1955 [Act 98]) may be petitioned through the Estate Distribution Division of Department of Director General of Lands and Mines (JKPTG), while movable-only estates up to RM600,000 may be administered summarily by Amanah Raya Berhad (AmanahRaya) under the Public Trust Corporation Act 1995 [4][5][12].
  • No Malaysian inheritance tax, but stamp duty and income tax remain: Malaysia imposes no general estate or inheritance duty, though the executor or administrator must clear final income tax affairs and arrange land-office transmission or Real Property Gains Tax clearances where applicable [4][5].

contacts.name: National Registration Department (JPN)
contacts.note: Processes ordinary and late death registrations and issues official Death Certificates across Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah, and Sarawak.

contacts.name: Department of Director General of Lands and Mines (JKPTG)
contacts.note: Administers small-estate distribution petitions involving immovable property under the Small Estates (Distribution) Act 1955 (Act 98).

contacts.name: Amanah Raya Berhad (AmanahRaya)
contacts.note: Public trustee corporation providing summary estate administration for movable-only estates up to RM600,000 and full estate administration.

contacts.name: Employees Provident Fund (KWSP / EPF)
contacts.note: Handles Death Withdrawal claims (Form KWSP 9KM) and Death Assistance applications for deceased members.

contacts.name: Social Security Organisation (PERKESO / SOCSO)
contacts.note: Administers Survivors' Pensions and Funeral Benefits under the Invalidity Scheme.

contacts.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs Malaysia (Wisma Putra)
contacts.note: Consular Division providing document attestation and legalization because Malaysia is not a party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention.
